title: Managing anxiety after completing treatment for primary breast cancer
official: Aligning Dimensions of Interoceptive Experience after Breast Cancer (the ADIE-BC trial)
summary:
Background and study aims
Many people continue to experience anxiety after completing treatment for primary breast cancer. Although treatments such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) can help, they do not work for everyone. This study is comparing two evidence-based approaches to managing anxiety after breast cancer. One approach provides information and practical strategies for managing anxiety after breast cancer. The second is a newer therapy called Aligning Dimensions of Interoceptive Experience after Breast Cancer (ADIE-BC). ADIE-BC is a mind-body approach that aims to improve how accurately people detect internal bodily signals, such as their heartbeat, and to help them use this awareness to regulate their emotions, reduce worry about normal bodily sensations, rebuild trust in their body after cancer treatment, and develop more helpful beliefs about their body. The study will compare these two approaches to find out which is most effective for reducing anxiety after breast cancer.

Who can participate?
Adults aged 18 years or older who have previously been diagnosed with stage 0–III primary breast cancer, have completed hospital-based cancer treatment and have at least mild anxiety.

What does the study involve?
The research team will complete a screening assessment to check whether the study is suitable for each person, as additional eligibility criteria also apply. Participants will first complete screening to check whether they are eligible. Those who take part will attend a baseline assessment at King's College London before being randomly allocated to one of two groups. Participants allocated to the ADIE-BC group will attend six face-to-face therapy sessions over approximately six weeks. These sessions involve computer-based heartbeat awareness exercises using a heart rate sensor, together with a handbook and practical techniques to help manage anxiety. Participants allocated to the Enhanced Usual Care group will receive a handbook containing information and evidence-based strategies for managing anxiety after breast cancer, together with a clinical check-in during the study. All participants will complete questionnaires before treatment, during the study, at 8 weeks and at 18 weeks after randomisation. They will also complete heartbeat tasks and provide saliva and blood samples at baseline and 8 weeks. Up to 80 participants may choose to take part in an optional MRI study involving two brain scans. Participants will also be invited to complete an optional questionnaire 12 months after randomisation.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may or may not benefit directly from taking part. They may experience improvements in anxiety or gain a better understanding of their body and emotions. Information gained from this study may help develop better treatments for anxiety after breast cancer for future patients. The study is considered low risk. Some participants may experience temporary emotional discomfort when discussing anxiety or completing questionnaires and behavioural tasks. Blood sampling may cause temporary discomfort, bruising or light-headedness. MRI scans (for participants choosing the optional substudy) may feel noisy or confined but do not involve radiation. Participants can withdraw from the study at any time without affecting their medical care.

Where is the study run from?
The study is sponsored by King's College London. Recruitment takes place through Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust, breast cancer charities and community organisations. Study assessments and therapy sessions take place at Guy's Hospital in London. Optional MRI scans take place at the Centre for Neuroimaging Sciences, King's College London.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
July 2026 to December 2028. 

Who is funding the study?
Wellcome Trust, UK.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Lauren Heathcote, Health Psychology Section, King's College London, UK.
conditions: Anxiety management in survivors of primary breast cancer.

interventions.name: Participants will complete baseline assessments before being randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to either ADIE-BC or Enhanced Usual Care (EUC). Randomisation will use a secure web-based system with stratified block randomisation and varying block sizes. Stratification factors are recruitment source,

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged 18 years or older
2. Resident in the United Kingdom
3. Able and willing to attend weekly sessions in London for 8 consecutive weeks
4. Able to read, write, and follow instructions in English
5. Have previously received a diagnosis of primary breast cancer (stages 0-III)
6. Have completed hospital-based cancer treatment between 6 months and 10 years prior to enrolment (long-term adjuvant therapies are permitted)
7. Meet criteria for at least mild anxiety, defined using a pre-determined cut-off score GAD-2 (≥2) (GAD-2: Kroenke et al., 2007)
Exclusion criteria:
Key exclusion criteria:
Unable to provide informed consent

Cancer-related exclusions:
1. Diagnosis of Lobular Carcinoma in Situ (LCIS) only
2. Diagnosis of secondary or metastatic breast cancer

Other ADIE therapy contraindications:
1. Previous participation in any ADIE therapy trial
2. Presence of an implantable cardioverter defibrillator and/or pacemaker
3. Scheduled to begin Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) during the intervention period
4. Health anxiety specifically related to cardiac symptoms or cardiac events where it is considered to interfere with ADIE therapy
5. History of severe cardiac events (e.g., myocardial infarction, sudden cardiac arrest, stroke) within the past 12 months where it is considered to interfere with ADIE therapy

Other physical health exclusions:
1. Pregnancy
2. Current substance or alcohol dependence where it is considered to interfere with ADIE therapy
3. Neurological diagnoses, including epilepsy, dementia, or Parkinson’s disease where it is considered to interfere with ADIE therapy

Other mental health exclusions:
1. Current medium or high risk of suicide intention and plan, determined by item 9 of the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and accompanying risk assessment questions
2. Current severe depression determined by Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8) (≥20)
3. Current diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), psychosis, or bipolar disorder where is considered to interfere with ADIE therapy
